A distributor once tried to negotiate a discount by saying the competitor's price was 'basically the same product.' It was not, in fact, basically the same product — a fact the samples made very clear within ten minutes.

A chess game at lunch once ran so long that the opponent had to resign not because of the position, but because the break ended.

A very formal client meeting was nearly derailed when the projector defaulted to someone's holiday photos instead of the slide deck. The beach photo got more engagement than the actual proposal.

meeting_casual: Opener: "Before we get into it — how's the week been on your end?" Costs nothing, buys goodwill.
If small talk stalls, ask about something concrete: their project, their travel, their team — not the weather.
You don't have to fill every silence. Let a pause sit for two full seconds before you speak.
A short, specific compliment lands better than a generic one: "that was a clean way to frame it" beats "good point."
If you're low on energy, one good question can carry the whole conversation — you don't have to talk more, just listen better.
Exit line for a casual chat: "Good catching up — let's pick this up properly next time."
You're allowed to say "let me think about that for a second" instead of filling the gap with noise.
Mirror the other person's energy slightly, not fully — match their warmth without matching their volume.
One well-placed question ("what's that been like for you?") does more work than three sentences about yourself.
If the conversation drifts to something you don't know, say so plainly: "I don't know much about that — tell me more."
A relaxed posture reads as more confident than a rehearsed sentence.
Ending on a specific note-to-self ("remind me to send you that spec") gives the conversation a natural close.
You don't need a joke ready. A genuine reaction is funnier than a prepared one.
If you're networking and drained, give yourself permission to have two good conversations instead of ten shallow ones.
"That's a good problem to have" is a solid, low-effort line for almost any minor complaint someone shares.
meeting_formal: Opening line: "Thanks for making time — I'll keep this focused so we can get to your questions."
State the ask early: "What I'm hoping we leave this meeting with is..." — it frames everything that follows.
When challenged, pause before answering. A two-second pause reads as consideration, not hesitation.
Bridge phrase for redirecting: "That's a fair point — and it connects to something I wanted to cover next."
If you don't have an answer: "I don't have that figure in front of me — I'll confirm and follow up today." Never guess out loud.
Closing line: "So, to summarize the next steps..." — always end with actions, not just agreement.
When presenting numbers, lead with the conclusion, then the evidence — not the other way around.
Handling pushback: acknowledge first ("that's a valid concern"), then respond with the fact, not the emotion.
If the room goes quiet after your proposal, don't rush to fill it — silence often means people are actually considering it.
For a hard ask: state it once, clearly, and stop talking. Don't undercut your own request by over-explaining it.
Transition phrase between agenda items: "That covers [X] — moving to [Y], the key question is..."
When you need buy-in, ask directly: "Can I get your agreement on this before we move on?" — vague nods aren't commitments.
If a meeting is going long, name it: "We have ten minutes left — let's make sure we land on a decision."
End every formal meeting with one sentence confirming who owns what, by when.
"Let me push back on that slightly" is a clean, professional way to disagree without conflict.
